pub.cite: Tan Q et al. Dual Hepatic Injury from Refeeding Syndrome and Starvation in a Malnourished Woman After Bariatric Surgery: A Case Report. Am J Case Rep 2024;25:e944088

title: Severe weight loss one year after bariatric surgery
sub: Refeeding syndrome followed by starvation-related liver injury after sleeve gastrectomy

pt.name: Woman, Tan 2024
pt.line: Sleeve gastrectomy a year earlier at 105 kg (BMI 37.2 kg/m2). Since surgery her intake has fallen sharply, with vomiting after high-protein foods and occasional self-induced vomiting. She has eaten about 400 kcal/day for several months and has had amenorrhoea for 9 months.

steps.v: Weight 33 kg, BMI 12.4 kg/m2. Electrolytes are normal. Fasting glucose is 3.2 mmol/L, AST 135 U/L, ALT 127 U/L and gamma-glutamyltransferase 187 U/L. Thyroid tests show a low T3 and T4 pattern, and gonadotrophins and sex hormones are very low. Echocardiography shows a mild to moderate pericardial effusion. She has been taking vitamin D, calcium and a multivitamin.
steps.q: How should nutrition support be started?
o: Treat as very high refeeding risk: give thiamine and a multivitamin before and during feeding, start at a low energy rate and build up over days, supplement phosphate, potassium and magnesium unless levels are high, and check electrolytes and clinical status daily
BMI is far below 16 kg/m2 and intake has been negligible for months; normal electrolytes before feeding do not lower the risk.
Electrolytes are normal, so start full requirements at 30 kcal/kg/day
Serum levels can stay normal in starvation while body stores are depleted; full feeding risks refeeding syndrome.
Withhold nutrition until the liver enzymes are normal
Raised transaminases are common in starvation itself and improve with careful feeding, not without it.
Correct the low glucose with a high-rate dextrose infusion, then start full feeds
A large carbohydrate load is the trigger for refeeding syndrome and raises thiamine demand.
steps.a: The team started 600 kcal/day (18 kcal/kg/day) as enteral nutrition plus diet. NICE CG32 classes anyone with BMI under 16 kg/m2 as high risk and advises considering a start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, and only 5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases such as BMI under 14 kg/m2, increasing to meet or exceed full needs by 4 to 7 days. It advises thiamine 200 to 300 mg daily with a multivitamin immediately before and during the first 10 days of feeding, and potassium, phosphate and magnesium supplements unless pre-feeding levels are high. The paper does not report whether thiamine or phosphate was given before feeding began.
g: Tan Q et al. Am J Case Rep 2024
NICE CG32. Nutrition support for adults: oral nutrition support, enteral tube feeding and parenteral nutrition. 2006, updated 2017
steps.p: Normal electrolytes before feeding do not mean low refeeding risk.
steps.dp: NICE CG32 likely daily requirements during early refeeding: potassium 2 to 4 mmol/kg, phosphate 0.3 to 0.6 mmol/kg and magnesium 0.2 mmol/kg intravenously or 0.4 mmol/kg orally. At 33 kg, 5 to 10 kcal/kg/day is about 165 to 330 kcal/day (calculated here). Count every source of energy, including intravenous glucose.

ok.cap: Vitamins first, a cautious start, electrolytes covered and checked daily.

bad.cap: A fast start: phosphate is pulled into cells and falls.

steps.v: Weight has risen from 33 kg to 34 kg. AST is 1,419 U/L and ALT 334 U/L. Phosphate has fallen from 1.04 to 0.63 mmol/L; potassium, sodium, calcium and magnesium are normal. She is very tired, haemoglobin and albumin are falling, and she bruises at puncture sites, with a prolonged thrombin time and INR and low fibrinogen.
steps.q: What is the most likely explanation, and what should be done?
o: Refeeding syndrome with liver involvement: reduce energy intake for a short period, replace phosphate, give thiamine and other vitamins, and monitor closely
Hypophosphataemia with weight gain soon after feeding began is the signature of refeeding syndrome.
Viral hepatitis: stop all nutrition and isolate her
Hepatitis does not explain the fall in phosphate, and stopping nutrition deepens starvation.
Liver injury from her vitamin supplements: stop all vitamins
Vitamins, especially thiamine, are part of the treatment of refeeding syndrome.
Not enough energy is reaching the liver: double the feed rate today
With phosphate falling, a rapid increase risks worsening refeeding syndrome.
steps.a: The team diagnosed refeeding syndrome on the unexplained rise in liver enzymes with hypophosphataemia after feeding began. They cut intake to 300 kcal/day (9 kcal/kg/day) as limited intravenous glucose and enteral nutrition, and gave phosphate, vitamin B and vitamin D continuously. Two days later AST had fallen to 789 U/L. The ASPEN consensus grades refeeding syndrome by the fall in phosphate, potassium or magnesium: 10% to 20% mild, 20% to 30% moderate, and over 30% or organ dysfunction severe, occurring within 5 days of reintroducing calories. Her phosphate fell by about 39% (calculated here), although it was documented on day 10. Tests for autoimmune and viral hepatitis were negative.

da Silva JSV et al. ASPEN consensus recommendations for refeeding syndrome. Nutr Clin Pract 2020
NICE CG32. Nutrition support for adults. 2006, updated 2017
steps.p: Phosphate falling after feeding starts: think refeeding before anything else.

ok.cap: Energy reduced for now, phosphate and vitamins given: enzymes start to fall.

bad.cap: The cause is missed and phosphate keeps falling.

steps.v: After the early improvement, AST climbs again to 1,216 U/L. Fatigue and weakness are worse, with leg oedema, abdominal distension and moderate ascites on ultrasound. Weight has fallen from 34 kg to 32 kg, albumin to 29.2 g/L and haemoglobin to 77 g/L, with no sign of bleeding. Phosphate stays low despite replacement. Ultrasound and elastography show no fatty liver.
steps.q: What should happen to her feeding now?
o: Recognise starvation-related injury from prolonged restriction: increase energy again in careful steps, continue phosphate, iron and vitamins, and keep monitoring daily
Falling weight, albumin and haemoglobin with a non-fatty liver point to starvation rather than ongoing refeeding injury.
Restrict energy further until the enzymes fall
Further restriction is what is now driving the injury.
Treat as autoimmune hepatitis with corticosteroids
Autoimmune and viral markers were negative, and the course follows the changes in energy intake.
Hold 9 kcal/kg/day and treat the oedema with albumin infusions and diuretics
This treats a sign and leaves the cause, inadequate energy, in place.
steps.a: The team concluded that she had starvation-induced injury (liver damage, severe hypoalbuminaemia and anaemia) from calorie restriction that was too strict. From day 21 they reintroduced nutrition at 700 to 800 kcal/day (22 to 25 kcal/kg/day) with continued phosphate, iron and vitamins. Weight rose, fatigue eased and AST fell from 1,216 to 98 U/L by day 38. The authors separate the two injuries by three features: hypophosphataemia (refeeding), the direction of body weight after feeding starts, and liver imaging (an enlarged fatty liver in refeeding, a near-normal liver in starvation). They add that a sharp fall in haemoglobin and albumin favoured starvation in this patient. NICE frames the low starting rate as a short phase, with intake built up to meet or exceed full needs by 4 to 7 days.
g: Tan Q et al. Am J Case Rep 2024
NICE CG32. Nutrition support for adults. 2006, updated 2017
steps.p: Calorie restriction for refeeding syndrome is a brief pause, not a new target.
steps.dp: When energy is cut for refeeding syndrome, write the review date and the planned step-up on the same prescription. Track weight, phosphate, transaminases, albumin and haemoglobin together: enzymes that rise while weight falls suggest too little energy, not too much.

ok.cap: Energy stepped up with cover: weight rises and the enzymes fall.

bad.cap: Starvation continues: the liver, albumin and haemoglobin worsen.

steps.v: AST is 98 U/L and ALT 105 U/L. She is gaining weight, and the fatigue has largely gone.
steps.q: What should the plan after discharge include?
o: A stepwise increase in energy intake with dietitian follow-up, continued vitamin and mineral supplements with blood monitoring, a weight-gain target, and psychological and bariatric team review of her eating and vomiting
Her malnutrition arose from an eating disorder after surgery; nutrition alone will not prevent relapse.
No follow-up: the liver enzymes are nearly normal
She is still severely underweight, and the eating pattern that caused this is unchanged.
Rapid catch-up at home on 3,000 kcal/day
A sudden large increase without monitoring risks refeeding problems again.
Reassure her that vomiting after meals is expected after sleeve gastrectomy
Persistent vomiting with extreme weight loss needs nutritional, psychological and surgical assessment.
steps.a: She kept an intake of 800 to 1,000 kcal/day after discharge. At one month she had gained 4 kg, haemoglobin had risen from 77 to 99 g/L, albumin from 28.8 to 36 g/L, and liver enzymes were near normal (AST 64 U/L, ALT 45 U/L). The authors advise that excessive early weight loss after bariatric surgery should prompt nutritional, psychological or further surgical intervention, and cite a recommended weight gain of 0.5 to 1.5 kg a week during nutritional rehabilitation. The paper does not describe the longer-term plan or her eating-disorder care in detail.
g: Tan Q et al. Am J Case Rep 2024
NICE CG32. Nutrition support for adults. 2006, updated 2017
steps.p: Treat the cause of the starvation as well as the starvation.
steps.dp: At discharge weight, 800 to 1,000 kcal/day is roughly 24 to 30 kcal/kg/day (calculated here). Agree the next energy step, a weekly weight target and the dates for phosphate, liver tests, full blood count and micronutrient checks.

ok.cap: Home with a stepped plan and a team: 4 kg gained at one month.

bad.cap: Without follow-up the pattern that led to admission returns.
